title: Negotiator was never called
article: Everything happened so fast, the two dozen RCMP officers surrounding a Saskatchewan motel had no time to bring in a negotiator before shooting one fugitive, RCMP officers said Wednesday.

Throughout Wednesday's testimony at the first-degree murder trial of Robert Sand and Laurie Bell, defence lawyer Greg Brodsky grilled police about the tactics used the day Sand's brother, Danny, was killed by an RCMP sniper.
In his questioning, Brodsky established that two dozen RCMP officers arrived at the motel and started to encircle it, but did not call in a negotiator.

Cpl. Darren Topping testified there was no time to take such a measure. The police had arrived only minutes before the Sand brothers and Bell started to move, Topping said, escaping out the back window, with Danny Sand going up on the motel roof.

"The environment was elevated to the point where the suspects were armed, barricaded and intent on hurting someone," Topping said. Negotiators are only brought in once a scene is surrounded, and that was still in the process of happening, he said. "We could not jeopardize and risk this person coming in."
The police had bullhorns, but did not use them. They did, however, shout warnings at the Sand brothers at various times, including at Danny on the roof.
"I'm certain he heard us," Const. Murray Chamberlin testified. "He looked right at us."
"Could you use a bullhorn?" Brodsky asked.
"At that point in time, I would have preferred to keep both hands on my rifle," Chamberlin said.

Robert Sand and Bell, his lover, are on trial for the first- degree murder of Const. Dennis Strongquill. Crown prosecutor Bob Morrison alleges that Sand and Bell were lovers on the run, and along with Robert's brother, Danny, were willing to do anything to stay free, including killing a police officer.

Laurie Bell was wearing an "excessive amount" of jewelry at the time of her arrest. She wore 21 chains, bracelets and necklaces, plus three crosses, nine gold rings, a nosering, and three watches - - a Bulova, a Gallet and a Birks.
As Bell was being searched, Const. Val Peever had to struggle to get off all the tangled-up necklaces and chains.
"It was an excessive amount of neck chains, bracelets and rings," Peever testified in court Wednesday.
The jewelry, Morrison alleges, came from numerous car thefts and break-and-enters during a 10-day crime spree in December 2001.

After the Strongquill shooting on Dec. 21, the Sand brothers and Bell fled to a motel in tiny Wolseley, Sask., 90 kilometres east of Regina. It was there that a shootout with the RCMP ended with Danny Sand dead, his brother and Bell under arrest.

In the threesome's motel room, the police uncovered a gym bag bursting with firearms, a shotgun and knife on the bed, shells and bullets strewn across the floor, a DVD player and DVDs, two bottles of hard liquor, and a single stuffed Teddy Bear, wearing a red Santa hat.
When Bell was taken into custody, she was shivering and weeping, testified Const. Lana Gregoire. In Bell's pants pocket, she had the key to the latest vehicle the group had stolen, a red S10 truck.
Robert Sand was quiet and calm after he was arrested, Const. Kevin Leach testified. His main concern was his brother.

Moments before Robert Sand was taken into custody, Danny Sand had been shot dead by a police sniper after he took up position on the motel's roof with a high-powered rifle and scope. Robert Sand did not witness the killing.
At the time, Leach told Robert that during the altercation at the motel, Danny had suffered a gunshot wound.
"It was fatal, right?" Robert said.
"Yes," said Leach.
Robert put his head down then, and chuckled. "Altercation," he said.
The trial continues today.

The Crown alleges the Sand brothers, Robert, 24, and Danny, 21, and Laurie Bell, 21, committed a string of crimes spanning three provinces, from Red Deer to Manitoba, stealing vehicles, robbing a bank and breaking into homes.
According to the prosecution, just after midnight on Dec. 21, 2001, Strongquill and his partner Const. Brian Auger stopped a half- ton truck after it ran a stop sign and failed to dim its lights.
As the two officers approached the truck, four shots were fired, hitting the cruiser in the windshield, hood and passenger door.
The officers got back into their cruiser and sped off, and those in the truck gave chase, finally ramming the cruiser, pinning Strongquill inside.
While his girlfriend allegedly shouted "kill him, kill him," Robert Sand then fired four blasts from a shotgun, killing Strongquill, the Crown says.
The three then fled into Saskatchewan, where police surrounded them later that day.
